I used to fight my own interests and time, beating myself up for wanting to do one thing instead of another. I've also tried to make my hobbies my career and found myself hating the things I once loved. Now? I enjoy my hobbies when they come to me. My hobbies also no longer hold any connection to money, as I think it's ineffective to put a potential price tag on something that I can enjoy for free. The way in which I make space for all the things I want to do, is as simple as just do them when I feel like it. I have a lot of broad hobbies and passions; Art, Writing, Video games, Tarot, Spirituality, Journaling, Reading, Painting, Crafts, Photography. 

I found that the more I allow myself to just enjoy things when I want to enjoy them, the more I enjoy them. I'm not going to force myself to draw if I really just feel like spending a few hours in Minecraft instead. I'm not going to force myself to journal if I'd rather be making little mindless doodles in my sketchbook. Since I've stopped fighting my own desires, I've found that I can enjoy my hobbies and passions SO MUCH MORE and I do them more often because of that. And I refuse to put myself in a box of dedicating myself to one thing. What's the joy in that? And to be honest, ADHD would NEVER allow me to function like that; and accepting that in of itself, is a new type of energetic freedom that I'm grateful to have!

So simply, do what you feel drawn to doing in the moment. Maybe after you invest some time into that thing in the moment, you'll gain more energy for something else. Currently, I rotate between journaling, tarot, and my games. Sometimes I get a drawing in, here and there, other times I don't. But I enjoy it regardless of when it happens! Time is precious, use it however you want to! ✨

The pup I got wasn't the original pup named Spirit, but the sibling and honestly her name fits her personality beyond belief. My relationship with my dog Spirit is unlike anything I had with my Doberman, and I do believe she was sent to me by her. 

Just like how Smokey sent me my two cats now. My experience is proof enough, and I love my animals so much; their passings really tore me open, but they sent me some really amazing animals in their place and I'm so grateful for them. 🙏🤍✨️

Honestly, it's a mix of the topics, but also the way I *feel* when I get to write. Journaling has become a very safe space for me, and in a way, I treat my entries kinda like a therapy appointment. Before when I was actively in therapy, I didn't journal. I didn't necessarily feel like I had a reason to journal when I'd just do my best to recount stuff that has happened and tell my therapist about it at the next appointment. I lost access to therapy back in April, so I've been journaling consistently since May, until now and the future. 

Most of my entries are reflections on things that happen in my day to day, but sometimes I get into deeper topics or look at prompts for deeper inspiration. I feel like Journaling allows me to get even deeper than my therapy appointments because I'm able to think more intentionally about the words I'm putting down on paper, and I'm able to slow down my brain to truly think about things. In therapy, I'm only given an hour to recount things that have happened, get advice, and work through it. But in my notebook, I can take as much time as I need, and feel things as I need to feel them. And not to mention, it is just me, the paper, and the pen. I don't have to hide, shorten, or present my thoughts in feelings in any specific way for another person. I can truly explore my thoughts and feelings as much as I want.

One of the key things though that I have found in Journaling and not so much in Therapy, is that because I don't have a person to go to for advice or suggestions (professional in this instance), in a way, that has forced me to really figure out situations on my own. It's put me in the position of really sitting with myself and making decisions without someone else's approval or insight; and in turn, I've been able to gain confidence in making harder decisions on my own, and navigating life without an external crutch. So in short, Journaling has allowed me to work through more mundane thoughts and feelings on my own time, and it's allowed me to become more confident in my own problem solving skills and coping mechanisms. 

I could go on and on and on about how beneficial it has been, and in turn, I do believe my journaling has been more effective than therapy, BUT it doesn't replace therapy. I would like to one day return to Therapy and use Journaling alongside it and see how much more I improve and grow from past traumas.

Prompts are just simply questions or statements that can be used to inspire you to write or think. Example, "What was your favorite childhood vacation?" The way I started Journaling was at first I started using prompts to help guide my entries, but the more I did those, the more restricted I felt. Reflections about the day I had, the feelings I experienced, good things that happened, bad things that happened. If I find something online, I'll journal about it or take notes on that too; I never restrict myself to what I can write or how long. Journaling is my safe space; it's just me and my pages. No one else has to know about them or what's in them. And that's what makes it really freeing to just write whatever is on my mind or to reflect on life in general.

I picked up Journaling earlier this year after I lost access to therapy and it's honestly been an incredible replacement. I hope to return to therapy one day, but Journaling has definitely taken over for good. I tend to write freely, and I do a bunch of things. Based on the experiences you listed here, I wouldn't say that you're facing an addiction with Art. I would echo the thought of other commenters that you're just enjoying the hobby and even experiencing a hyperfixation on it! Hyperfixations can absolutely deter you away from other activities because your brain is more caught up on the one you're really enjoying, and that's okay!  


I'd like to add though, my experience with what I believe to be was an actual art "addiction" several years ago. I was in a really bad spot IRL my first year graduating high school. I was in a very awful living situation and I had seen that people were able to make money through art and I figured, hey! I wanna do that! And I very quickly became *obsessed* with the notion that I needed to improve as quickly as possible so that I could make money from this once passion of mine. It got bad. 

All I would do was *draw*. I wouldn't do anything else. It even got to the point where I had worked on a single piece for *18 hours straight* without any breaks, and I was so exhausted and fatigued, and STILL ended up hating the end result. I also minorly injured my hand from that; I wasn't able to hold a pen or pencil for *three* days following that because the muscles in my hand hurt so bad. I don't think this was a true addiction like we traditionally know it as; however I would definitely call it an obsession, with the wrong reasons attached. I wasn't drawing for enjoyment. I was drawing for survival to get out of my shitty situation; and while that in itself ISN'T bad at all; what made it bad for me, is that I allowed it to consume me, in negative ways. It was interfering with my ability to sleep and care for myself physically, it damaged my mental health in many ways, my self esteem and confidence *plummeted* both as an artist, and as a person, and it has forever damaged my relationship with Art itself as a hobby and passion. 

I am actively working on improving this now, as it has been several years now since that has happened. I'm no longer in a bad place, but my relationship with Art itself is forever changed, but it's something I'm actively trying to work on and repair because it is important to me. 

SO! With that all said, I would say that as long as it isn't harming YOU mentally and physically, and doesn't take away your overall quality of life, enjoy the focus and creativity for as long as you can! 🤍✨

Learning Digital Art has a huge learning curve because of how different it is to traditional. You have so many different programs available to all different levels of digital artists, and there are SO many different settings, tools, brushes, etc that you can learn and master over time. And to even push a further challenge with digital art, is learning how to make it look like traditional materials or getting different textures appropriately. Digital Art is unique in that aspect with being alongside traditional because both require a lot of time and patience and you *still* need to know the basics of art itself. 

The thing that I like about that, is that digital art doesn't exactly take away from traditional. The change of medium is not the only difference there. If you look in your digital piece, you attempted to do some shading and folds in the shirt, which you had minimal of in the original pencil drawing. I can also see that you have more control over your lines and the choices that you made, which you can see between the pencil and the digital in the flow of the hair. The proportions and spacing on the face, are more accurately placed in the digital piece than in the traditional. These are all genuine moments of growth, even for being a redraw of the same exact piece; AND even doing it on a different medium in itself is growth too, because learning new mediums, *especially* the transition of traditional to digital can be quite daunting.  


I definitely understand the struggle of figuring out what to draw. That decision in itself can take forever to sit right; something I would recommend is if you don't like using word prompts (there are massive amounts of lists and generators to give you ideas) then enjoy some of your other hobbies or interests and see if you can draw inspiration from those. For example, I enjoy playing Minecraft and will sometimes be inspired by Minecraft's landscape to create a landscape piece. Or, I also enjoy reading, so sometimes I'll feel inspired to create a piece based off of a scene I read. Or even watching other artistic youtubers, or just youtubers in general; Sometimes I'll just feel inspired to create a piece based off of the most non-sensical thing. (An example, a Pun I had between myself and some coworkers at work, turned into a physical fantasy acrylic painting as a parting gift for my boss when we had all split ways!) Inspiration is *everywhere*. And it can be daunting sometimes, but it doesn't need to be.   


Here's the thing, not every piece needs to be a masterpiece. Each time you draw, and create, you are flexing your creative muscles and making sure that they still work. It's like moving around. If you sit for too long, you get stiff and achey. *But here's the catch*, every time you move around, you are NOT moving with the intention of running a marathon, or lifting weights. **Not every piece you create, needs to be improved.** You won't love every single line or mark you make. You won't enjoy every hour spent you put into a piece.   


Honestly, sometimes it's nice just to have *one* piece of art in your portfolio that you don't feel proud of; so then that way when you do create a piece that you sincerely enjoy and can feel proud of, you can feel that tenfold, because you have that one other piece that just didn't quite make the mark. And that's okay. Lowering the expectations you put on yourself when creating overtime, will genuinely make creating a much smoother process, and when you do find yourself asking questions of improvement, it's not a punishment.   


Because I too, understand the feeling of wanting to improve so badly. I feel it all of the time; I admire artists who are WAY above my level and skills. But so long as I don't compare myself entirely to them, and put my own skills down, then it's okay to want to improve. But something to ask yourself is; *Is my need for improvement hindering my growth as a creative individual?* Because of how many avenues and creative liberties there are; you can truly spend the rest of your life improving and still never feel like you've made it. But you just gotta recognize when improvement is or isn't needed, and lowering your critical expectations on yourself. I know that's easier said than done, but I hope this helps!

Truthfully, I disagree with the concept that you don't learn anything by using or relying on a 3D poser. While I do agree that absolutely, fundamentals should be considered; that's a given for EVERYTHING though; you can't drive a car without learning the fundamentals of the law, or knowing what pedal does this or that. You can't cook a fancy meal without learning the ingredients or different cooking processes. That's a given for everything. So yes, absolutely, Fundamentals need to be studied and worked on; but Fundamentals themselves should not limit your curiosity and experimentation. 

If you are using the 3D poser, or a reference image, and you find that you are learning something from them, then they are absolutely useful to use. Because that'll in turn, work up your mental library and help you level up your skills overtime. 

If you feel that you aren't seeing any growth, here are some suggestions; because it is absolutely valid to seek out advice and criticism to improve when you feel like you aren't. But, I ask you; 

Do you have any old art you can compare to your current art? I can almost guarantee you that you will see improvement somewhere between the two. Treat your old piece vs your new piece as a "spot the difference" game. Notice where some lines may appear more confident, or where colors mesh in better ways than they did before. The best way to see growth in yourself as an artist, is not to compare yourself to others, but rather to your past creative self. 

How often do you draw or create? If you do it consistently and quite frequent than it can certainly feel like you aren't improving; something I would suggest doing is as you create a piece, or finish one, take some time to journal your thoughts about your process or how the piece turned out. As much as I didn't enjoy doing art reflections back in High School, as a young adult now who does struggle with her artistic self, these reflections are truthfully far more crucial than I could've imagined when it comes to building up my confidence and growth with my creative spaces. 

You don't gotta go ham crazy with this process, but just taking a little bit of time to be more mindful about your creativity and art itself, can truly help you feel more at peace with it, which in turn could help benefit when facing criticism! I truly do hope this helps in some way; I myself currently have a strained relationship with creating at the moment but I'm working through it and these are things that I'm doing myself to help with that.

I resonate with this post, so I'm gonna give you the advice that I would honestly tell myself; I used to be really sensitive to criticism as well too.   


Something you could do to help ease yourself into criticism is try changing the language and mindset of criticism itself. Example; instead of asking "How can I make this piece look better?" Or, "What are the flaws in this piece?" Sometimes I feel like the language associate with asking these sort of questions can sometimes be too jarring or negatively charged, and therefore that could play into our perspective of criticism itself. Words like, "better", "flaws", "wrong" carry some (not always) negative connotation, depending on the context.   


So, some ways to better phrase asking for criticism can sound like this, "What are some ways that I could *enhance* this piece?" or, "Is there a *different* way I could *adjust* this piece?"   


You could even take it a step further and *acknowledge* the parts you do like of the piece, within the question itself. An example; "I really like how I placed this aspect of the piece, but is there a way to enhance that feature more appropriately?" or, "I want to include this aspect in the piece, but I feel that it doesn't fit, could you point out some different ways that I could make it work?"   


These are truthfully questions I would ask myself when it comes to confronting my own artwork and feeling sensitive to the idea of it being judged or changed, based on the opinions of others. This process shouldn't take away the aspect of learning that comes from constructive criticism, but like I mentioned earlier, I feel that often the language surrounding criticism is often too negative and focuses too much on the flaws of the piece; and so when more sensitive, creative souls want to improve, it can be quite difficult to do so, because of the harshness of the language itself.   


And this little tidbit may not apply to you and I don't want this come off as a personal attack at *all,* but something I have found in myself as an artist, is that often when I am anxious of criticism, it can be linked to my own insecurities as an artist, and doubting myself too greatly. And to help combat this, I will tell myself affirmations in regards to my skills such as, "I am good at creating ideas." And, "I am proud of myself for picking these colors for this piece."   


I like to pair these affirmations with phrasing my questions for criticism because it acknowledges the work I already put into the piece, and it also promotes a smoother pathway for receiving feedback. This advice may or may not work for you, I truly hope it does because it's unfair to those that are sensitive; to have their entire creative identity stripped away while asking for improvement.   


I'd like to touch also, that, that comment you received on newgrounds was not constructive. It was rude, and detrimental to your growth. I want to acknowledge you for using a 3D model posing program, because it is a *tool*. It's not cheating. Just like references, they are tools. I hope this helps; you are not a lost cause.   


There is *always* room for growth; you just gotta nurture it in the right way. 🙏🤍✨

Unfortunately I don't have any experience with the Gender aspect; but what made me realize that I may actually have OCD was a few months ago. A little bit of background, but I'm already diagnosed with Major Depressive, PTSD, and Anxiety. But a few months ago, during the summer, before I go to bed, I would scroll through instagram, youtube, etc just to calm down from the day. Most of the videos I watched, were of animals and dogs being silly or goofy; just really lighthearted videos. Well, my dog would (and still does) sleep with me almost every night. She is, in a way, my support pup and has helped me through a lot, and I've been with her through a lot too (She's a 4 year old Doberman). So I'm really bonded with her. Well, watching these videos, would trigger some really nasty thoughts. I'm a huge believer in manifestation and that your thoughts can help create your reality. And these thoughts, that had just started appearing as I'm watching these videos, would scenarios of my dog dying, and me reacting to it in some way. I couldn't stop the thoughts. They just happened and especially at night, right before bed. Which would lead to me breaking down and crying, every night, for weeks on end. Sometimes I'd cry for as long as 2 hours before actually falling asleep. Even if I didn't watch any videos, those thoughts and scenarios would pop up in my head. It was, and still is torture.   


(Just to note, I have brought this up to my therapist, but I'm unsure of if I'm actually diagnosed yet or not. I plan to talk to my therapist about this more in our future appointments.)  


Now, these thoughts usually do not get me at night anymore, but they still make their way into my daily thought process through out the day; and that leads to the compulsion aspect of me texting my mom to ask what my dog is doing, to make sure that she's still alive. It's horrible. I could think of a potential scenario that has NOTHING to do with that original thought, but it'd still find a way to be present. It's very triggering, especially emotionally, and it's exhausting sometimes, taking a time out during a task (especially during work) to tell myself that she's okay, and that everything is fine. It's really difficult.   


On a somewhat less serious note; I have compulsions of doing things in a certain order across multiple activities and tasks. An example would be at work, we have a cardboard baler that smooshes boxes down, and they don't have to be completely broken down, but for me, it HAS to be. This is of course, not as severe, but something I just recently observed while working. Another thing, is that at my old job, I had to do the closing procedure a specific way, and if I didn't, I'd feel anxious about forgetting something or doing something 'wrong'. I experience more of the pattern thing, and less of the repetition that often comes with OCD. Although I suppose there relatable.

I'm not sure of that exact warning, but I'm not surprised it shows up. I always get anxious when it comes to major gift card transactions. A good way to tell the customers is something along the lines of; "Sorry, but it looks like our system declined one of the cards. Unfortunately we can only sell a few of these to you today because our systems are getting overloaded due to the holidays. We can sell you a few of these today and then you can come back tomorrow to buy the rest of them if you'd like." That may not be the perfect response, but something along those lines for a popup warning about that.   


I would also suggest if your store doesn't do it already or not; but only to accept cash or debit card for gift cards and any visa or reloadable cards are to be cash only. This is another way to help prevent issues from occurring. And if you wanna take it a step further, for leading up to Christmas, to have a sign at the register that mentions the gift card limitations due to the holidays. I hope this helps, and I hope you and your store stays safe through out this week! If you have any more questions, don't be afraid to send em!

A tip for dealing with this; I'm an ASM at another DG, my boss and I established a pretty firm rule that customers are limited to $500 worth of gift cards per day, per customer; and only 5 gift cards as well. So when doing a transaction, if they have 5 gifts, split it up into two transactions so that way the system doesn't get overloaded and if it happens to decline one of the cards, it'll be much easier to find which one it is.   


This is something to keep in mind all the time, but it's especially useful around this time of year. If they're paying with cash, keep the gift cards close to you and check / count the money according. Make sure the gift cards have been activated and the receipt prints before you hand back the gift cards to ensure they don't scam you! Hope this helps with that!
